topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Playing with numbers
topic.scope: factors and multiples, prime and composite, divisibility rules, HCF and LCM, prime factorisation

misconceptions.statement: The number 1 is a prime number.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the definition of prime (exactly two factors) with the uniqueness of 1.
misconceptions.fix: A prime number must have exactly two distinct factors: 1 and itself. 1 only has one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

probe.question: Which of these is a prime number: 1, 2, 3?

misconceptions.root_belief: definitions are flexible based on number size

misconceptions.statement: To check divisibility by 3, look only at the last digit.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the rule for 2, 5, and 10 to all divisibility tests.
misconceptions.fix: The rule for 3 is to add the digits of the number; if the sum is divisible by 3, the whole number is.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: HCF of two numbers is always smaller than both numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse HCF (Highest Common Factor) with the concept of a common multiple.
misconceptions.fix: The HCF is the largest factor that divides both numbers, so it can be equal to the smaller number but never larger.

probe.question: What is the HCF of 5 and 10?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: All odd numbers are prime numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students notice that 2 is the only even prime and 3, 5, 7 are odd, so they overgeneralise that oddness means prime.
misconceptions.fix: Odd numbers like 9, 15, 21 have factors other than 1 and themselves, so they are composite. A prime has exactly two factors.

probe.question: Is 9 a prime number? Why or why not?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 9 is prime because it is odd.

misconceptions.statement: 2 is not a prime number because it is even.
misconceptions.why: Students learn that even numbers are divisible by 2, so they think every even number is composite, forgetting that 2 itself has only two factors.
misconceptions.fix: 2 has exactly two factors, 1 and 2, so it is prime. It is the smallest and the only even prime number.

probe.question: Is 2 a prime number?
probe.wrong_answer: No, 2 is even so it is divisible by 2 and is not prime.

misconceptions.statement: The factors of a number do not include the number itself or 1.
misconceptions.why: Students think of factors as the 'smaller parts' that make up a number, so they leave out 1 and the number itself.
misconceptions.fix: Every number is divisible by 1 and by itself, so both are always factors. For example, the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
misconceptions.root_belief: Factors are only the proper inner parts

misconceptions.statement: The multiples of a number are the same as its factors.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the words 'factor' and 'multiple' because both relate a number to another by multiplication.
misconceptions.fix: Factors divide the number exactly and are finite; multiples are the numbers you get by multiplying it, e.g. multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16...

probe.question: Write the first four multiples of 6.

misconceptions.root_belief: Factor and multiple mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on factor-multiple confusion in school maths

misconceptions.statement: A number is divisible by 5 if its last digit is 5 only.
misconceptions.why: Students remember only the example 5, 15, 25 and forget that 0 as last digit also gives a multiple of 5.
misconceptions.fix: A number is divisible by 5 if its ones digit is 0 or 5. So 40 and 120 are divisible by 5.

probe.question: Is 70 divisible by 5?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it does not end in 5.

misconceptions.root_belief: Rule applies to one example digit only

misconceptions.statement: Prime factorisation of a number can stop when the factors are any two smaller numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students follow the multiplication step procedure without understanding that every factor in the final answer must itself be prime.
misconceptions.fix: Keep splitting factors until all of them are primes. For 36, 6 × 6 is not complete; 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 is.
misconceptions.root_belief: Any factor pair counts as complete factorisation

misconceptions.statement: The HCF of two numbers is found by multiplying them together.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse HCF with the product of numbers, or take multiplication as the default way to combine two numbers.
misconceptions.fix: HCF is the greatest number that divides both exactly. List common factors or use prime factorisation and take common primes. HCF of 8 and 12 is 4, not 96.
misconceptions.root_belief: Combining two numbers means multiplying them

misconceptions.statement: The LCM of two numbers is the larger of the two numbers always.
misconceptions.why: Students see examples like LCM of 4 and 8 being 8 and generalise, ignoring cases where neither divides the other.
misconceptions.fix: The LCM is the smallest number divisible by both. It equals the larger number only when the larger is a multiple of the smaller. LCM of 4 and 6 is 12.
misconceptions.root_belief: Special case results apply to all cases

misconceptions.statement: Bigger numbers always have more factors than smaller numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students use whole-number thinking that larger size means larger count, ignoring structure like primes.
misconceptions.fix: Number of factors depends on the number's structure, not its size. 97 has only 2 factors while 12 has 6.

probe.question: Which has more factors, 97 or 12?
probe.wrong_answer: 97, because it is the bigger number.

misconceptions.root_belief: Larger number means more of everything

misconceptions.statement: Multiples of a number stop after the multiple of 10, like a table.
misconceptions.why: Students learn multiplication tables only up to 10 and think the list of multiples ends there.
misconceptions.fix: You can keep multiplying by 11, 12, 13 and so on forever, so multiples are infinite. There is no largest multiple of 5.

probe.question: What is the largest multiple of 5?
probe.wrong_answer: 50, because the table of 5 ends at 5 × 10.

misconceptions.root_belief: Multiples end where the table ends
misconceptions.source_hint: research on finite-infinite concept in number theory
